B_source.statement:
Let $f: A \to B$ and $g: B \to A$ be [[Definition:Injection|injections]].
Then there is a [[Definition:Bijection|bijection]] $A \to B$.
This is the [[Cantor-Bernstein-Schröder Theorem]].

derived.the two injections: a bijection between P(N) and R

object_map.reformulation: Find an injection in each direction and apply Cantor-Bernstein-Schröder.

validity_conditions: Density of Q makes the cut map injective.
Ternary expansions using only the digits 0 and 2 are unique, which makes the second map injective.
proof_plan:
The map $x \mapsto \set {q \in \Q: q < x}$ is an injection $\R \to \powerset \Q$, by density of $\Q$.
Composing with a bijection $\Q \to \N$ gives an injection $\R \to \powerset \N$.

The map $A \mapsto \displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop \in A} 2 \cdot 3^{-n - 1}$ is an injection $\powerset \N \to \R$, as ternary expansions with digits $0$ and $2$ are unique.
Its image is the [[Definition:Cantor Set|Cantor set]].
By the source result, there is a bijection $\powerset \N \to \R$.
